utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, all. I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and we are joined with two interns, Ms. Louise Beck and Paul Derohannesian, appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin, there's a small housekeeping matter and this relates to the, quote/unquote, informal request that we received, Mr. Hannis, and what we've decided is that the -- we would take a 30-minute break from 5.30 so that would result in the third session being abridged by 15 minutes. Of course, all this is subject to the -- any problems that the witness himself may have. So we go from 2.15 to 3.15, 3.30 to 4.30, 4.45 to 5.30, and then the final session is from 6.00 to 7.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I announce that there is a small matter which I was requested by the Trial Chamber to address yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do we have to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honours, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Macar. I give you the usual reminder about your solemn declaration before I invite Mr. Hannis to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, when we left off yesterday, I think we'd been talking about briefings and collegiums of the MUP that you attended in 1992. And in that connection, you had told Mr. Zecevic last week on 6th of July that at these meetings you all reached some conclusions that the influence of local bodies of government, the Crisis Staffs and the War Presidencies, was "overbearingly influential" is the translation I have of your term. And I wondered, did you have knowledge of or can you tell us any specific examples of a local police chief or an SJB receiving from a Crisis Staff and carrying out an order to do something illegal. Did you have any evidence that that was happening between the local Crisis Staffs and the local SJB and SJB chief?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have information that SJB chiefs received orders to commit crimes. I do have information, though, that SJBs were tasked to do something from the remit of municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said -- you also said in your answer that later on in the year when you were doing some of your inspections or your tours out in the field that -- that you were being told that some Crisis Staffs were making decisions that police officers were to be sent to the front line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any document to show us where a Crisis Staff ordered policemen to go to the front line?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have documents that show such orders. But I remember an example. When we had a meeting with the representatives of the crime enforcement services of the Sarajevo centre, I forgot which event triggered it, but, anyway I asked the chief of the crime enforcement service at Sokolac to explain, to give me some instructions, and he looked at me with confusion, and he said to me, "Boss," that's they called me, "Boss, I came from the front line yesterday." And I asked him, "What do you mean?" I know that the crime enforcement service still isn't fully manned. And I -- I wanted to learn about the way things went. The Sokolac municipality was affected by combat activity in the direction of Olovo and the front line was pierced repeatedly. The Crisis Staffs that -- which, at the time, took care of security issues demanded that the police be engaged at the front line. And it's important for the Trial Chamber to know what the problem was with these engagements. The VRS had 15 days of leave after 15 days on the front line; whereas, police officers, after one day of rest or even without any rest, after coming back from the front line had to go about their policing duties. Based on this information and the way they were engaged - and I'm now referring only to crime enforcement - I told the minister that something must be done about the way the police were sent to the front line, because if a police officer is at the front line 15 days and goes about policing duties in the following 15 days, it's very difficult to do his work efficiently because he has no information about what went on in the meantime, where he worked. Because the crime situation in any given area had to be monitored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just inquire with the witness something that he said a while ago, when you asked him whether he had examples of either the SJB or the local police chief being asked or ordered by the Crisis Staff to carry out something illegal. Mr. Macar, you answered that you had no information that SJB chiefs were being so asked but that you did have information that some SJBs were tasked to do something from the remit of municipal authorities. That's what you said. What -- what were those things that the Crisis Staffs will asked the SJBs to do? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me first comment that I said in my statement that I didn't have information that SJB chiefs received orders to commit any crimes. But what is outside the remit of an SJB, such as municipal services, providing security, or acting as couriers or running errands, receiving refugees and assisting in these segments; certainly, if a thousand people turn up somewhere, that's a problem. Although there was the Red Cross and other organisations. So there were many administrative duties, much administrative work, that had to be done by other structures, municipal bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There seems to be some misunderstanding here. Because I thought that Mr. Hannis was asking you if you had any information that SJBs, one way or another, would be engaged in illegal activities because of orders or instructions or demands being made by the Crisis Staffs. So I just want to clarify a bit what sort of activities are we talking about here? Illegal activities, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Illegal activities or activities contrary to the minister's orders are something that I can explain on the example of Samac. Our inspectors found out that, pursuant to the orders of the Crisis Staff, some police were engaged to provide physical security for the collection centre at Samac. That was in contravention of all orders, but it was ordered by the Samac Crisis Staff, and the police took part in that. They were involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just how was that illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army had the duty to provide security to such facilities, and the MUP had no need to do this kind of work. Additionally, there were the minister's orders saying that police cannot be engaged to do something from the remit of the army, unless some police are resubordinated to the army in accordance with the procedures that were in place. In other words, if those units were to join army units and then do this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you have other examples of illegal activities done by the SJB at the instigation of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of the year, I was informed that it was similar in Prijedor. Pursuant to the orders of the Crisis Staff in a similar way, police forces were engaged, although they had instructions or, rather, orders as to how they should conduct themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macar. I think this is as far as I can get with this. Back to you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, let me ask, first, a couple of specifics about the example you gave concerning Sokolac and the inspector who had been at the front line. When was that; do you recall what month in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the inspector?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, it was Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall his first name? We've got another Borovcanin who's an inspector.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his first name, but I'm certain about his family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there not some military command of the VRS that was working in the area of Sokolac at that time; and, if, so do you know which unit it was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there was a military unit in every municipality and it had its command. I don't know anything about their organisation or their formation or structure or anything like that because that was outside my remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask is, wouldn't it have been the VRS that was resubordinating a policeman who was going to the front line rather than the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the front line is pierced in a war or when the enemy is launching offensive operations, then the army reacts with all available capacities. They may or may not have enough reserves at that time. The Crisis Staffs, being informed of the problems at the front line, demanded that the police forces be engaged to the highest possible extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I would like to show you the Law on Internal Affairs and ask you about a provision in there relating to the Crisis Staffs and the local police authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit P530. This was tab 3 of the Prosecution's list. And if we could go to page 4, both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I want to direct your attention on the screen --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll blow it up --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this is poorly legible, and my eyesight isn't so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll blow it up and hopefully you can see it. I want to look at Article 27 in both English and B/C/S. How's that? Can you read it now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My translation reads: "In addition to the activities and tasks set out in the Rules on the internal organisation of the ministry, a public security station shall implement regulations passed by the municipal assembly and relating to law and order ..." So let me ask you: Does that mean -- and, first, let me ask you this question. This talks about municipal assemblies. But would you agree with me that in times of imminent threat of war, or war, or a state of emergency, that the Crisis Staffs stand in the place of municipal assemblies. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so for purposes of this Article when it says "municipal assembly" I'm talking about Crisis Staffs. The way I read that, it sounds as if the Crisis Staff passes a municipal ordnance or a regulation relating to law and order, then the public station shall implement that. So if a Crisis Staff decides because of the war time situation that they need to have a curfew or they need someone to provide security at the hospital because you may have an enemy prisoner in the hospital being treated and you're afraid that locals may come in and cause a disturbance, that's something that shall be implemented by the police; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to read this Article out loud ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't need you to. I don't know if the Judges need to you to. We have got it on the screen. We can all read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I am wondering whether the witness wants to do it for his own comprehension. If he's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that's the case, then I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If it's convenient for him. Then you may proceed, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read just this part after the coma after the word "ministry." "... a public security station shall implement regulations passed by the municipal assembly ... relating to law and order ..." Could you please bring it back. "... and road safety," as part of the assessment of the situation in the sphere of law and order, the municipal assembly or the Crisis Staff may issue a decision prohibiting the opening or, rather, the operation of various catering facilities or restricting their working hours, and the police - because this is a decision that pertains to law and order - has to act. They have to act if a catering facility operates in contravention of this decision. The same goes for road safety. If a decision is issued that a -- trucks should not use a specific road, then traffic police must act. Municipal decisions of this sort can be taken by the assembly, and other tasks that have nothing to do with law and order and road safety could not be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then, isn't it a matter of interpretation of -- about whether or not in the circumstances existing at the time a particular measure has to do with law and order?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that establishing a curfew could relate to the law and order during the context of an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, based on the assessments of the public security stations, about any disturbances of law and order, especially if it can cause danger to general public or some other kind of danger, then a curfew could be established, and the police was supposed to implement this decision by stopping citizens who happened to be outside during the curfew and to check what their reasons are, and file criminal -- or, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Misdemeanour reports, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, could you look at the phrase for me and tell me what you understand that to mean. Because it says: "... regulations passed by the municipal assembly and relating to law and order and road safety ..." And then it says: "... as well as other regulations in the domain of internal affairs ..." What does that mean? Can you give me an example of a regulation that would be in the domain of internal affairs that doesn't relate to law and order and road safety?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really recall, and I don't want to speculate. But I actually read this in another way, that the municipal assembly cannot issue decisions that are not in line with the Law on Internal Affairs. Well, the municipal assembly can issue a -- decisions to discuss on a monthly basis or every three months, every five months, or annually, the security situation in its territory and that the public security stations should report to it covering the period determined by the municipal assembly. It can be one month, three months, five months, and so on. It is up to the assembly to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me follow on in this discussion about Crisis Staffs and the local police. You said one of the conclusions that you all at the ministry collegiums reached was -- and this is at transcript page 22899, line 23: "The heads of public security stations should, as a matter of priority, inform the Crisis Staffs of their work." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the -- that's not what I said, that this was a priority for them to report. But in line with the decisions because, I noted a little while ago, it is only natural for the Crisis Staff to discuss security in the area, in the territory of its municipality and it is quite natural for the chief of the SJB to report about the work of the station itself and to take measures to improve the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well -- I wondered about that at the time when I read that answer on the transcript. Did you mean to say that you, at the collegium, had concluded that the heads of public security stations should, as a matter of priority, inform the CSBs about their work instead of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the translation is wrong and never a decision was made at the collegium that these heads of the SJBs should inform anyone about anything, report about anything. That was not a topic at any of the collegia. When I spoke about that, I said that at the collegium we would talk about the impact of the Crisis Staffs on the functioning of the public security stations. And now I would like to add that in some municipalities, there were some problems that some people advocated at the time because they did not understand the whole system. Well, some people in the municipal authorities wanted to impose military rule, to suspend civil rule. And in many municipalities there were problems of this sort, and this definitely had an impact on the functioning of the ministry. They may have acted more as if they were part of a military rule. They brought together civilian and military aspects of power together, and that is why the police was involved to such an excessive extent in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Try and be patient with me here because I'm trying to clarify what you said last week, and all I have to go by is what is in the transcript in front of me. And I'm still not sure, then, what you meant to say when you said: "One of our conclusions was this: The heads of the public security station should, as a matter of priority, inform the Crisis Staff of their work." Now I understand you're saying, no, no, that was never said. But you went on to say: "And for the most part, they weren't informing the Security Services Centre or the ministry of the interior in situations where that was required." And then you say: "There are two aspects to this. One was a technical aspect. It was physically impossible to communicate with the centre, or the minister, the HQ. That is part of the reason why they had to communicate with the Crisis Staffs." Do you remember giving that answer to Mr. Zecevic last week, on the 6th of July? And if that's not correct, can you tell us what you meant to say there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to hear an audio-recording of what I actually said. It seems to me that we were talking about the problems that the Ministry of the Interior faced in its work, especially the SJBs and the CSBs. And I do think that I said, at the time, that the problems of keeping the ministry headquarters and the minister informed and keeping the CSB informed by the SJBs were caused, for the most part, by technical problems that we had. And that with some of the public security stations we would have a situation that the chiefs mainly kept the Crisis Staff informed rather than the relevant centre from which the reports would go onto the ministry or to report directly to the ministry. I think this is the gist of my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That makes sense to me. And you know that in most places that I am aware of, the SJB chief, the local SJB chief, was a member or a participant in the local Crisis Staff. Didn't you find that to be the case in 1992 in the RS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not directly a member of anything, but the reports that we received and the reports that we received from the collegium made it clear to me that in conditions where the Crisis Staff assumes the role of the municipal assembly, the chiefs report on the security situation in the area covered by their SJB to the Crisis Staff. Now, whether there were any SJB chiefs who were involved in the Crisis Staffs, well, I can't really tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, do you personally know of any Crisis Staff in the Republika Srpska in 1992 where the local SJB chief was not a member or not a regular attendee of Crisis Staff meetings? Can you tell me one municipality where that was the case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just told you that I can't tell you whether there were any, and if there were any, how many of them were involved in the Crisis Staffs. And according to the normal procedure, it would be normal for the SJB chief to report to the Crisis Staff about any security problems because the Crisis Staffs assumed the role of the municipal assembly, and that would be fully in line with the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs, because that's the security-related issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. That reminds me I meant to ask you about one other provision of the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, if we could look at this document that's on the screen. But if we could go to Article 31 which is, I think, on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Macar, I will ask you if this is it what you had in mind. My English translation says: "If so requested by the municipal assembly and its executive committee, a Security Services Centre and a public security station shall submit reports, information, and other data relating to the situation and problems in the area ..." Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Were you aware that, apart from the communications system that the MUP was using, that the -- the Presidency and the government had access to a communications network that was primarily based in Pale and it was sometimes called the republic communications centre. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Related to the problem with local Crisis Staffs having too much influence over the local police, at page 22900, you said: "Most of the people in leading positions, the chiefs and heads of public security stations were never appointed by the minister but, rather, by the local Crisis Staffs. And that was probably one of the most important reasons why the Security Services Centres were unable to have a consistent subordination system, in terms of the way they functioned." Can you give me an approximate total number of how many SJB chiefs there were in the Republika Srpska in 1992? Was it 50, 100; do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you of the list for September that I did. There were 73 public security stations, which means that there were 73 public security station chiefs, commanders, chiefs of crime enforcement sections and so on, and all the other elements that were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any idea of that number of 73, how many of those had not been appointed by the minister or were not subsequently approved by the ministry? Was it 10, 20; do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be a question for the chief of the legal affairs and personnel service, because I did not have statistical data in my service. But I do know that there were quite a few chiefs who had not been appointed in accordance with the procedure of the Ministry of the Interior, which required that the centres recommended them for the appointment and then the ministry approved it, and that is why in 1992 attempts were made to re-establish procedure in line with the law and the appropriate order of the minister in this sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the -- of the CSB chiefs, of which we understand there were five - Trebinje, Doboj, Sarajevo, Banja Luka, and Bijeljina - do you know how many of them had appointments from the minister in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably appointed all of those chiefs. And their files show us whether he signed the appropriate decision or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to your answer where you said that security centres were unable to have consistent -- a consistent subordination system, for purposes of this question, don't -- don't include Teslic SJB and don't include Prijedor. Apart from those two, can you give me any specific examples of a SJB chief refusing to subordinate to his CSB and follow orders and provide requested information, demand -- disband the special unit when required to do so. Can you tell me any other example?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some examples where the leaders of the autonomous regions disbanded the special units, if you're talking about the disbanding of the special units and not -- and other issues. But I'm not aware of any other examples -- or, rather, I cannot recall any of them. I probably did get reports about that at our meetings, but I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we're still on the one-hour schedule, I guess it's time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we resume in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way in, there is a matter which both as an issue of courtesy and efficiency, I should have brought to the attention of counsel today. Counsel may have picked this up from other sources, but in terms of the resumption of the present trial after the break, it is now projected that the other trial in which this is running in parallel would run for three weeks and, therefore, the -- counsel would recall that we had previously projected a two week/two week alternate sittings. What is now expected to happen is that the other matter will run for three weeks, then we will resume this case on the 5th of September for three weeks, and, thereafter, the two week/two week plan would -- we would revert to the two week/two week originally planned. And any alarm that counsel may feel would be relieved then on reflection, you would realise, we probably are at the end of the day in a better position than we would have been with the two week/two week arrangement. So, therefore, any rumours you have heard to effect that, I have now confirmed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, the next topic that Mr. Zecevic took you to was asking you about the fact that we'd had in this trial a number of documents suggesting that war crimes committed against Serbs were singled out for -- for priority on investigations, et cetera. And he showed you, and I think I talked with you earlier about that document from the federal Ministry of the Interior in -- from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in April 1992, where they were requesting from your newly created MUP information about war crimes and international law crimes where Serbs and other ethnicities were the victims. Do you recall that document and that discussion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I can -- I can show it to you in a minute. If I recall what number it was, but I don't recall off the top of my head. While we try to find that, let me ask you a related question. In your answer, you said: "In 1992 there was much propaganda. The Serbs were represented in various ways, very bad ways, which you probably know. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs wanted to present the situation on the ground as realistically as possible." Do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was propaganda of the other side. That propaganda, for a great part, was not founded on facts. Anything not on any information that we had. But what exactly is your question you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to show you another document that I think is related to the one that we looked at before. Let me show you that now while I'm still trying to found the old one. And this one is P173. This is tab 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one that the Prosecution just e-mailed this morning, one of two additional documents we wanted to add for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Macar, this is a document dated the 16th of May, 1992 to the various Security Services Centres. It has Mr. Stanisic's name and a signature on it. And you'll see the number of this, Witness, is a strictly confidential document. This is the 01-2/92. And in the first paragraph he makes reference to a task resulting from the order by the minister, strictly confidential number 01-1, dated the 15th of May. I will remind that you 01-1/92 strictly confidential was the one where Mr. Stanisic is talking about creating war units in the ministry. You remember us looking at that one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when we were explaining this strictly confidential tag.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to look at page 2 of the B/C/S, and it's page 3 of the English. It's Roman numeral IV, war crimes. It says: "Measures and activities conducted to document war crimes. These activities must involve collection of information and documents on war crimes against the Serbs. This implies conducting an on-site investigation with the entire team in all cases of crimes against the Serbs." And at the end of paragraph you will see it says: "In order to send copies to the federal SUP and the Federal Secretariat of the interior of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." This to me seemed to be related to that other document that we had seen from the Federal Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry, I -- I note that there might be a mistake in the translation. Perhaps the witness can -- can read the very first sentence that you -- the very first two sentences that you wrote -- that you -- that you read from -- from the translation, so we can have the accurate translation of what is said in the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Macar, maybe you can help me out. I have read what I have in English in front of me. But it is a suggestion that that's in error. So could you please read the first few lines of paragraph Roman numeral IV?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph IV, war crimes: "Take measures and activities to document war crimes. These activities must involve collection and -- of information and documents on war crimes against Serbs."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness did not read out the first sentence as it is printed in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I -- need I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The interpreters interpreted exactly as it is stated in the translation. However, I insist that they interpret what they hear and not look at the translation what is written. It is similar but it's very different you see, Your Honours, because there is no word "must" ever mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we just got word from the interpreters that apparently what the witness read out was not similar to what is in the B/C/S text. So maybe we should try once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a bit puzzled by this. I heard the interpreters over the headphones say that the witness did not read out what is printed on the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's the first word of the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, could you repeat for us that exercise and start from the first -- first word under war crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Take measures and activities to document war crimes. These activities need to involve information and documents about war crimes against Serbs."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness again did not read out the first sentence as printed in the document. The first word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think even at that, the gist is generally the same. However, I would request that we submit this to CLSS for a revised translation, since this one is a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Macar, the point I want to make is, this is a direction to document war crimes against Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of this document is that measures are being taken and activities were under way to document war crimes, as stated in the first sentence. Without making a distinction between war crimes against Serbs, Croats, Muslims, or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how can you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wait. Wait. How can you say that, sir? Because it says "war crimes against Serbs." It doesn't say "all war crimes," or "war crimes generally," or "war crimes against all ethnicities." It says "war crimes against Serbs"; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, please. Show me where it says "against anyone besides Serbs." It says "against Serbs," doesn't it? It doesn't talk about war crimes against any other group; right? Can you answer that "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may, Your Honours, I'll be glad to finish my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would request that you ask him to answer my question which calls for a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Hannis, your question, your original question was whether this is direction so-and-so correct. And he began by saying his understanding is, and he went on. So having posed the question the way that you did, you mightn't be satisfied with his explanation but can he only answer according to his understanding. So he should be permitted to complete the question as he understands it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my first question was: "Is this a direction to document war crimes against Serbs; correct?" And then he said his understanding was it was to document war crimes without making distinction. And then my question was: "How can you say that, sir? It doesn't say 'all war crimes.'" So my question is now what does the document say on its face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the witness is about to explain his understanding. Now you may come back to this if you aren't satisfied with his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first sentence, it is clearly stated "take measures and activities to document war crimes." The second sentence follows, and it reads: "These activities must -- need to involve the collection of information and documents about war crimes against Serbs." The first sentence means that war crimes must be documented. And I believe it's clear enough. And the second sentence says that, as part of this work on documenting war crime, information and documents must be collected that have to do with war crimes committed against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you read the next sentence for us, please, so I'm sure I'm working from a correct translation.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sentence saying that information and documents must be collected about war crimes against Serbs, and it is continued like this: "This implies conducting an on-site investigation with the entire team in all cases of crimes against Serbs ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You can stop there. Is it your understanding of that phrase that it does not require an on-site investigation with the entire team when the war crime was not against Serbs. Isn't that the logical inference?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is like this. According to the Law on Internal Affairs and the Law on Criminal Procedure, it is clear how the organs of the interior proceed. In the second part, which mentions crimes against Serbs, does not mean that the same procedure should not be applied in case of crimes against other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then, why is it being specifically pointed out that in all cases of crimes against the Serbs, there should be an on-site investigation with the entire team, if an on-site investigation with the entire team is standard procedure for all cases? Why is it needed to be said that this applies to cases of crimes against the Serbs, unless there's some reason to make a special emphasis?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely do not understand this document as something that states that a different procedure should be applied in case of crimes against members of other ethnicities. I don't know who wrote this document on behalf of the ministry, but I can say that in May 1992, there was a rampant campaign against the Serbs in the media and somebody from the ministry may have requested some material to present the situation on the ground as different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, and I think you've said that before, that -- and because of the perceived campaign to portray Serbs in a bad light, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Presidency and the FRY were interested in trying to counteract that perception. But in doing so, I suggest to you, Mr. Macar, that the emphasis was more on public relations than actually solving crimes against non-Serbs. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. We do disagree. Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before you go to another document, Mr. Macar, could I ask you to read, ones again, the two first phrases of this document under -- under the title "War Crime." I want -- I want to listen to the French translation. Would do you that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Take measures and activities to document war crimes." End of sentence. "These activities must need to involve the collection of information and documents about war crimes against Serbs." And if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'd like you to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If -- if Mr. Macar wants to add something, please do, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I understand in the Serbian language is the following: There are two activities in this request. One is to take measures and activities to document war crimes; and, secondly, as part of these activities, war crimes against Serbs should be documented, and documentation is sought to complete it all. That's how I understand it in Serbian. And that's how I originally understood this document and not as a distinction or discrimination to deal only with one group of crimes, or one type of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Macar, I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, there's a question which Mr. Hannis put to you and to which I believe I understood your answer, but I'm going to phrase this slightly differently. And it is this: Appreciating, as you have explained, that this directive about taking measures would have been of general application, why was it necessary, in this paragraph and the portions that Mr. Hannis has cited, to specify any particular ethnic group; in this case, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that two or three times during the examination by the Defence I was explaining that there was constant pressure or there were constant requests made to the ministry to submit, among others, information about the suffering of the Serbian people in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only in the RS. Not only dry information was sought to be presented to international representatives and so on, and then what followed, there was additional elaboration that, among all the crimes, there were also crimes against Serbs and as evidence there are medical documents, photographs, or other documents, such as witness statements, and so on, to serve as an illustration to counteract that propaganda, and vividly show that crimes had been committed against the Serbian people in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, then, let me point you to two things. The end of that paragraph says, in my English translation: "... in order to send copies to the Federal Secretariat of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, among other things?" So this information, one of the purposes of gathering it is to send it to the Federal Secretariat of the Interior in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Among other things, in order to submit copies to the federal SUP." And, as far as I know, at least as far as the crime enforcement administration is concerned, I don't remember that such information was sent to that secretariat in 1992. Whether or not it was done by another service, I don't know. But the crime enforcement administration certainly did not compile such material for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to put it all into context, could we go back to page 1 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that first paragraph, halfway through, my English translation reads: "And in order to collect documentation on the crimes against the Serbian population (for prosecution and to accurately inform the local and international public), fax reports must be submitted daily to the ministry ..." Doesn't that also indicate that the emphasis here is on crimes committed against Serbs? Wasn't that the priority?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't understand this as setting a priority. It's an explanation why -- it was explained later, in fact, and it says quite clearly here: "In order to inform" -- just a moment, "... the domestic and international public." So this is the reason why the other part was explained. It would be much more logical. It would appear to be much more logical if we had seen this first, because it's an explanation of the other segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macar. And now, you had asked to see the document that I think this relates to. And that is 1D635, Defence tab 14. I'll show that to you and just to make sure that's what we were trying to talk about. And while it's coming up, I will tell you it's dated 22nd of April, 1992, from the federal Ministry of the Interior. Or that Federal Secretariat of the Interior; I'm sorry. Do you remember seeing that one the other day? Because I had a discussion with you then about why there was a distinction about crimes committed against Serbs and other ethnicities. Do you recall this document now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the last one we just looked at from the RS MUP, Mr. Mico Stanisic, appears to be a response partly to this request for information about war crimes and other genocide and international law crimes committed against Serbs? Don't those two seem to be related, this document and that one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree with this part, that only Serbs were the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: As of 22 April 1992, the newly created Republika Srpska, or I guess at that time, it was called the Serbian -- the Republic of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm sorry, I can't keep track of all the names. But your newly created republic was not a part of the FRY, was it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see that the decision that was made at the session of the federal council of the 18th of March, the decision was made on the establishment, scope, and composition of the state commission for collection of data for the verification of war crimes, crimes of genocide, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that the commission was created before the conflict began in Bosnia. But as of the 22nd of April, isn't it fair to say you had no legal obligation to provide this information to the FRY; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for whether we had a legal obligation, I am a crime policeman. I wouldn't like to go into that. I think it's something for a -- law scholars to answer. And as I've already told you, I don't know whether in 1992 - I'm now talking about the crime police - crime enforcement administration, that we submitted any reports. Now whether anyone submitted such reports on behalf of the ministry, I can't tell you that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You would agree with me, though, wouldn't you, that in April of 1992 you guys had plenty of problems more serious than sending a report to a country that you didn't have a legal obligation to send anything to. You were in a war fighting for your very existence; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, I did have problems much greater than the ones described in this document. Where to find accommodation for my family, how to make ends meet for my family, and, as far as I can remember, this was the beginning of the war, and I can tell you that I myself and 90 per cent of my colleagues were convinced that something would happen to prevent the situation that existed in the field and that the combat operations, the fighting, would not continue. Because I, my family, and most of my colleagues, and I think the Serb people as a whole, did not want the war. We don't -- didn't want the fighting to continue. That's what I can say about this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P625.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is tab 63 from the Prosecution's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just looking at the first page, this is dated January 1993 and appears to be to the annual report on the work of the RS MUP for the period April to December 1992. Have you ever seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was discussed at a collegium meeting in 1993. I would like to have a copy in the Serbian language too, a hard copy, because it's very difficult for me to read because of the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic helpfully has one available. If the usher could hand it to you. Thank you. And I want to go to page 14 of the English, and in e-court, the B/C/S is e-court page 20. I think for you, Mr. Macar, in the hard copy, the page number you need to be looking for at the bottom is page 17. And, actually, if you look back to page 16 on the previous page, you'll see a portion underlined. My English translation says: "The work of the service for crime prevention and detection ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we need to go back one page in e-court. No, we're on the right page; I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, on the left-hand page. It says page -- 16 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. And you see the underline heading: "The Work of the Service for Crime Prevention and Detection." That's your administration; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at this time, in December 1992, I think when information for this report would have been collected, you were at least, de facto, acting head of that administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, were you involved in any way in providing the information that went into this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was drafted on the basis of the information that we received from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I -- I think I've heard testimony that this report was actually prepared by people in the -- in the 10th Administration, the analysis people; is that correct? That Mr. Vujic's [sic] administration.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that right? Were they the ones who would have put this together?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Based on the information that came in from the centres and the SJBs, this was all put together into this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did it work in terms of creating the final product? Because you were the acting head of that administration, did you get to see the draft of what was being said about the work being done by the crime police and make any changes or additions? Did you have a chance to do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information that was submitted by the CSB and what the administration had been doing in 1992, an overview of the whole situation, this was all submitted to the analysis section where the report was drafted. At least that's how it was done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if, after the report is written, you read the part that pertains to your administration and you see something that's not correct, do you have an opportunity to make a change or have a supplement filed so that there's an accurate picture of your section's work, your administration's work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this report was drafted in late January for the collegium, as it existed at the time, well, I did not have an opportunity to review it because in February 1993 I spent 90 per cent of my time in Belgrade because my wife was there for her first surgery. My late wife. So I can't really tell you. I see that this is January, and that this is a draft version, so it may have been completed in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that it's time for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could return to the MUP annual report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Macar, I'll going to read a couple of sections and ask if -- if they're accurate or if you would agree. On that page where we have the heading for the work of the crime prevention, paragraph says: "In the first stage, at the beginning of April, the main activity was the evacuation of crime prevention officers from the MUP of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina to Vrace and the setting up the operational groups and crime departments in public security stations in the area of Republika Srpska." And would you agree with that? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had I drafted this document myself or reviewed it, I would not have described this stage in April in those terms. And I can be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a question first. I understand you say you wouldn't agree with it, but is it inaccurate? I understand you may have written it differently. But as it's phrased, is that not true and correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior, as we have already stated so many times, in the Buducnost building what you asked me about Kalovita Brda. And in April, the ministry, now whether it was on the 20th or sometime in April, moved to the building in Vrace, in mid-April, or after the 20th of April, it was in the building in Vrace. And I would like to correct this: The evacuation of the crime prevention officers from the MUP of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would disagree with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, remind us again: Where were you between the 3rd of April and the 19th or 20th of April? Where were you personally located?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have already stated, in Sokolac until my late wife and my children, my family, left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you weren't at Vrace in the first couple of the weeks of the war, so you don't know who was there, do you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I know most of the members of the crime enforcement service from the Sarajevo area, I had an opportunity to learn how and when they left their places of residence, not the MUP, because from Sunday or Monday, 90 per cent of those employees could not do it because of the fighting and because of their concern for their families. They could not go to work, because this is what the situation in the town was like. For most of them, in particular the operatives who lived in the suburbs of Sarajevo, there were quite a few of them, it was impossible for them to go to work, physically impossible, to MUP. That's why I disagree with this phrase, "evacuation from the MUP." If it said gathering the employees who had fled the parts of Sarajevo held by the other side, well, then, I would agree with that, and that's how I would phrase it, because that is a fact. And if I could ask you, since I see that this is a draft version, I would like to ask whether we have the final version, because I can see that this is the draft version. That's what it says on the front page. Because a final version would bear an appropriate number. Here where it says strictly confidential, copy number, you would have the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this is the version we have. I don't have another version to show you. But I want to ask you, I'm not sure I understand your disagreement. This document says: "... evacuation of crime prevention officers from the MUP of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina." I take that to mean that Serb -- Serb policemen who had been working in the joint MUP before the conflict started were evacuated to Vrace. You disagree with that? You don't know that Mr. Planojevic went to Vrace briefly in early April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when Mr. Planojevic was in Vrace. But I wanted to know where he was when he left for Vrace and that was definitely not -- he was definitely not in the office where he worked, and I don't believe that on the 6th of April he was in his office and that he was able to go to Vrace. The terminology used here "evacuation of crime prevention officers from MUP" at the time when the two warring factions already had taken their positions and when it was basically impossible to pass through, I failed to see how anyone could evacuate them. Now, the Serb side organised the evacuation. Well, in that period, it was only possible to use your connections, your friends, among the Croats in Stup to cross from the area where Serbs were in the majority, and those were isolated cases. I'm talking about citizens in general who wanted to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your disagreement. Let me move to the next paragraph and read you a sentence there. "The second stage was characterised by the relocation of the MUP of Republika Srpska to Pale municipality." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had written this, I would have said the MUP in the headquarters, not of the entire MUP, but the MUP that existed in the headquarters that was located in Vrace. So it was not the entire MUP that was moved to Pale. The minister, with the rump administrations, if I can call them that, moved from Vrace to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And skipping the next sentence, to the third sentence in that paragraph said: "This period of the UZSK," that's the crime prevention and detection administration, as I understand it, "was not characterised by organised criminal operative work." You would agree with that, wouldn't you? You weren't able to carrying on your general organised operative work in this early second stage?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, where it says that this period of the UZSK was not characterised by organised criminal operative work, this means that the crime enforcement administration was supposed to be set up with the appropriate personnel and equipment, and, as we have already said, because of the shortage of personnel and equipment, the administration was not set up and it was unable to perform its function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next paragraph says: "The third stage began with the relocation of the MUP headquarters to Bijeljina." That's accurate, isn't it? That was the next stage for MUP headquarters, was the move from Pale to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then it says: "Only then was the criminal police administration, with organised and planned work on the tasks of crime prevention and detection, actually set up and posts filled." And then there's a footnote with some more information about that. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My explanation for this part, had I been involved in the drafting of the report, it -- I would say it was only then that the activities commenced to set up the crime enforcement administration, and it started taking shape. And from this, it would appear that, once the headquarters moved to Bijeljina, everything was done, and this was not a process that could be completed on the day of the move or within five days of the move, definitely. And that is why I fear that this is just a draft version that was amended at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By whom? Do you remember making any changes to this draft report? Who would have amended this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that this is January. That's when this draft version was produced, and it was probably finalized in February. And as I have already said, in February, I was absent. I only came to Bijeljina very seldom, in order to obtain medicines for my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if this section of the report dealing with your administration was amended sometime after this was written and it wasn't done by you, who would it have been? Did you have a deputy or somebody immediately covering for you when you were gone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know. At the beginning of the question, I said I didn't know if it had been changed. This was a draft. Whether or not anybody changed it, I don't know. That would be speculation. The Trial Chamber had the opportunity to see yesterday, based on a document that was presented, that we were able to look into the archives of the crime police. I wanted to prepare and make sure that I can give adequate answers based on documents, and I would have found documents there that pertain to the crime enforcement administration. Unfortunately, I must inform the Trial Chamber that the request was never acted upon because I only found out almost half a year after my inquiry that the top officials of the MUP were afraid that somebody would be accused of aiding and abetting war criminals. It would have been helpful to me, though, and good for both the Defence and the Prosecution, because I would have been able to find my way through the documents better than anybody else, and I would have been able to observe whether there was anything missing and check the continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I share your despair about not having a complete set of documents. Let me ask you about the next paragraph. It says: "In this period, the criminal inspectors visited all the CSBs and SJBs and had meetings where they gave instructions for carrying out concrete operative activities." Is that right? I know you were trying to visit all the CSBs and SJBs with the available personnel during the last part of 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with the part that says that the focus of the operative work in CSBs and SJBs was" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, Mr. Macar, you're reading ahead. I wasn't asking you about that sentence yet. You're awfully anxious to get to that part about the Serbs, but my question was the first sentence about your inspectors visiting all the CSBs and SJBs. Is that part accurate? We'll get to the next one in a minute.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you told us previously that your inspectors went out and visited many CSBs and SJBs in the latter half of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they visited some centres and some stations. Not many stations. The reports clearly show which ones we did not visit, especially the 24 stations from the area covered by the Banja Luka centre. Some of the stations belonging to the Sarajevo and Trebinje centres also remained unvisited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now we'll get not next sentence which says: "The focus of the operative work in CSBs and SJBs was on detection, documenting, and reporting members of the enemy army who had committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people, torched or destroyed immovable property, cultural and religious monuments, and other assets." That's correct, isn't it? A focus of the work, the operative work in the CSBs and SJBs, was about crimes against the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among others. I would never say the focus of operative work. Yes, one of the tasks was to submit reports about members of the enemy army that had committed crimes against the Serbian people, and this applies to combat zones. The focus of the operative work of CSBs and SJBs certainly wasn't only on this, on such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go over one page in both the English and the B/C/S. Actually, I think it may be on your page number 18, Mr. Macar. Yes. You see there's a paragraph is that said: "The administration" -- sorry. "The administration has, in particular, provided expert assistance and direct operative engagement to take measures and activities in investigating criminal activities in the work organisation TAS in Vogosca since the beginning of war operations." That investigation about the stolen cars and the stolen Golf vehicles from Vogosca took a big part deal of your administration's time in 1992, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question first and then you can elaborate. Can you name me three other investigations that your administration did in 1992 that took more time, more men, more resources than the TAS investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the work of crime enforcement isn't measured by the amount of time spent on something. The TAS case went on throughout the war and continued after its end. All centres had their own remit and conducted checks in their area. At the beginning, when the Sarajevo centre initiated these activities and took them over and took part in all meetings about how they should proceed, everybody was checking operative information in their respective areas, and it is the task of crime enforcement, since, towards the end of the year, we were able to reach agreement with the Serbian MUP, the MUP of Serbia, to forward information to them about vehicles that were supposed to be stolen from the TAS factory. That doesn't mean that all the operatives worked 24 hours a day on that case. There were operative workers who checked some information and that information was obtained during four years of the war and even after the war, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think you answered my question, though. Could you tell me three other investigations that your administration did that took more time and more resources than the TAS investigation. Can you name one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer briefly. First of all, this was not an investigation of the administration. The administration assisted the Sarajevo CSB in the operative implementation of the TAS case. And when an operation is conducted, especially about stolen cars, the information is forwarded to other centres and stations where there was possibly information that they were registered based on forged documents. That is, all stations through their administrative and legal departments checked whether vehicles with certain engine numbers and VINs were registered in their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Macar. We'll move onto something else. You were asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but perhaps it's a misunderstanding, because I'm listening and I see that the witness is not answering your -- your question at all, and he keeps -- he keeps giving explanation about the TAS, and that was not the question, and ... I wonder, because I don't have my earphones, I don't know what -- what -- what was the translation that he got. Maybe he is confused about the contents of your question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think it's a very confusing question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, did you not understand? I was asking you if you could name -- well, first, I asked if you could name three other cases investigated in 1992 that took more time and more resources than the TAS case; and when you seemed to have difficulty answering that, I asked you if you could name one case that took more time and resources? Do you understand that question; and can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security Services Centres and public security stations were working on solving all sorts of crimes observed in their area. How can you measure how much time was invested into solving, I don't know, the Yellow Wasps case, or case A, or case B? We assessed these things based on how difficult it was to apply the relevant methods to collect information and evidence and not based on the time used to obtain them. I believe that this may be clearer. And this is mentioned in the context of economic crime, because an economic operator was harmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't want to spend any more time on this, Mr. Macar. But the Yellow Wasps, you could have some measure of how much time was spent on that case but counting up, what, 14 operatives did 59 interviews over a period of seven days and come up with a rough estimate of how much time was spent on the case; right? I see you shaking your head no. I'll take that as a no and move on. You were asked about what happens when -- when the police file a criminal report, send a case to the prosecutor's office. And you pointed out that the characterisation of a crime depended on the evidence and that the prosecutor could change the classification of a crime if he or she thought that was appropriate. Do you personally know of any case where the MUP submitted it as a war crime and the prosecutor changed the designation to something else that was not a war crime? Did that ever happen in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have insight in the subsequent activities of the prosecutor's office; that is, we don't know whether the prosecutors changed the classification of a crime. So I have no relevant information because their work was not open for inspection by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've mentioned a lot about the problems with Crisis Staffs and their independence from the higher level of government. You were aware that there was a transition beginning in June 1992. The Crisis Staffs were disbanded and replaced by, first, War Presidencies, for a day or two, was what was in the -- in the legislation, but then it was changed to War Commissions. You knew about that change in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were amendments to the laws, but I cannot specify how the dynamics of that process went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you know that one of the changes from Crisis Staffs to War Commissions was that the War Commission established in a municipality included some representative from the republic level government? For example, in Zvornik, when they created a War Commission at the end of June, beginning of July, Dragan Djekanovic, a republic minister, was a member of the War Commission. Did you know about that facet of War Commissions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I took no interest in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you see how that was one way in which the central government, the republic government, was trying to get better control over those local municipal authorities, to make sure that what was being done at the local level was consistent with what they wanted to do from the republic level. Seems a logical way to go about it; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could speculate about it. But since I didn't attend government sessions, nor did I follow the implementation of their decisions, I'd rather not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, regarding Crisis Staffs and -- and local situations, at page 22912, you mentioned that there was an incident which took place in Prijedor sometime in November that caused me to look into the situation and the conduct of senior staff members. When you say an incident in November, are you talking about the occurrence when you went to Prijedor and had that brief meeting with Mr. Drljaca when he basically sent you and your colleagues away? Is that the incident you were talking about there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only time in 1992 when I was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I assumed it was. I just wanted to be sure there wasn't some second incident. And you were shown, in connection with this, Exhibit -- well, 65 ter number 619D1. That's Defence tab 57. And it was a list of conclusions and decisions by the Crisis Staff and the Prijedor Executive Committee relating to the SJB. I can give you -- oh, do you have the tab there? I think it's tab 57 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me take a look at the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You recall looking at that one before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, for example, number 4 on the first page talks about a conclusion of 30 June. And the second paragraph under number 4 talks about company directors are supposed to be responsible for implementing this conclusion relating to the ownership of socially owned flats that had been vacated. And then it says: "The chief of the SJB and the regional command shall be obliged to take the most rigorous measures against any members of the police or military who have broken into flats." Now, there is nothing wrong with the Crisis Staff or the municipal assembly asking the chief of police to take measures against policemen who have broken into flats; right? That's not interfering with the work of the police, is it, to ask them to basically do the job of the police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station, under the Law on Internal Affairs and the Law on Criminal Procedure, is duty-bound, because, under these two laws, it must act. And if they have information that a member of that station has broken into an apartment, they must take measures to file a criminal complaint and initiate the procedure to suspend these members. But that isn't done pursuant to such a conclusion. That's regular procedure. I believe that if the municipality had information that somebody had done something like that, they could submit according information, but a public security station works pursuant to the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I would say, at best this measure by the municipal assembly or by the Crisis Staff is unnecessary, but it's not really an inference with the work of the police, is it? It's just asking them to do what they're supposed to do under their own law. Is it your position that this is meddling and interfering with the work of the police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's interesting that the municipality is giving orders to the SJB through this conclusion, ordering it to act under the Law on Internal Affairs. If they had an information, then there's a procedure in place how that information is -- is submitted, or forwarded. I've already explained how a public security station is supposed to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note it's time for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, because -- in order to accommodate certain commitments that counsel have, this is a slightly shorter session. We have a longer break, so we would resume in a half-hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would suit me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one more question about this Defence tab 57, 65 ter 619D1. It seems we have something different on the screen at the moment. I think it's -- it's at the bottom of page 1 in the English, and for you, Mr. Macar, it's item number 1 under the heading: "A Summary of Conclusions, Orders and Decisions from 29 May to 24 July."
