The first one order number such and such of 5 June forbidding the unauthorised firing of fire-arms on municipal territory, and it says the competent organs of the military police and SJB organs are tasked with implementing this order. Now we looked earlier at Article 27 and the Law on Internal Affairs, which says that SJBs are -- shall implement regulations passed by municipal assemblies or Crisis Staffs related to law and order. Would you agree with me that forbidding the unauthorised firing of fire-arms on the municipal territory is something related to law and order?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it had nothing to do with the Crisis Staff, the executive function of the authorities in the municipality. This is a typical example. If you discharge a -- fire-arms, this causes public danger, and this is sanctioned in the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Criminal Code, where organs of the interior routinely intervene because this is within their purview, within their jurisdiction. Or it's the military police that has -- intervene if it is within their jurisdiction. And as all the other items listed here, this is yet another example of assuming this -- the functions on the part of the executive branch, the Crisis Staff, or the Executive Board, and you could see that in the previous examples where they issued orders to the military and demanded reports from them, and routinely reports are received from the public security station and reports are filed, listing all the -- all such cases, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I held my hand up because the interpreters requested that you repeat the last part of your answer. I'm afraid that you've gotten away from them again.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how far they got.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Neither do I. But let me ask you this: I'm not sure if you disagree with me or not. It seems to me that this kind of ordnance or regulation passed by the Crisis Staff is something that is related to law and order. And under Article 27, the public security station shall implement it, according to the Law on Internal Affairs. Do you -- do you have some quarrel with that? How is this interfering with the work of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that. The Crisis Staff had a problem with that. Things that are regulated by the Law on Public Law and Order, the Law on Criminal Procedure is not under the jurisdiction of the Crisis Staff. Or, rather, it cannot make decisions about those elements that have already been regulated by a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you point to me some law that says that the Crisis Staff or the municipal assembly can't pass a local municipal ordinance that may already be regulated by law? Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on Public Law and Order, the Law on Misdemeanours, the Law on Criminal Procedure, regulated crimes and misdemeanours which are dealt with by the organs of the interior. And now imagine a situation where somebody gets mixed up as regards their role, and they say, No crimes shall be committed in the territory of my municipality. Yet you have such a provision in the relevant law already. And in this sense, this is in line with the way in which administrative organs function. It is ridiculous for a Crisis Staff to issue an order prohibiting the discharging of fire-arms when there is such a provision already in the law. The law already prohibits it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. Let me give you an example and ask you to compare it to your experience. In my jurisdiction where I grew up, there would be a federal law against the sale of marijuana, and that would cover the whole United States. And there would be a state law in the state of Arizona that prohibited the sale of marijuana, and there might be a city ordnance in Phoenix Arizona prohibiting the sale of marijuana. Now why is it a problem for the municipality to pass a regulation even though there may already be something in the RS Criminal Code or the federal Yugoslavia Criminal Code? Where is there a provision that says the municipality cannot pass a local ordnance banning the same kind of conduct? Can you give me a specific statutory or constitutional provision that says that's not permitted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the Crisis Staff issues an order, and in its order it charges the organs of the SJB and the military police with performing tasks that are within their purview under the law. The municipal assembly itself cannot task -- cannot issue decisions that are already regulated by a number of laws, such as the Law on Criminal Procedure, Criminal Code, Law on Misdemeanour. They cannot issue orders that are covered by those laws, and it -- apparently we have totally different legal systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you keep telling me that they cannot but you haven't been able to tell me the place where I can find that law. Is it in the constitution of the Republika Srpska? Is it in the Criminal Code? Can you give me -- cite me an article, a law, a number, where I can go look it up?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Try and find the Law on State Administration which regulates the actions of all the relevant organs from the state all the way down to the municipality, and you can read there what the government is in charge of, what the Executive Board in the municipality is in charge of, and you will see that they are not authorised to issue this kind of order. This tells us more about the way in which the executive board actually operated because they assumed all the legislative power. They controlled the army and the police. They assumed power over them in contravention of the regular procedure because in the chain of command, the chain of reporting in the MUP, that's how the reports were supposed to go. They were not supposed to report to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One final question on this and then I'll move to another topic. You saw Article 27 which said that public security stations shall implement regulations passed by the municipal assembly relating to law and order, traffic safety, and other matters falling within the purview of internal affairs. Are you saying that Article means the municipal assembly, or the Crisis Staff, can only pass regulations that cover matters that aren't covered by some other already-existing law? Is that is that how you read Article 27 of the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked about the problem related to the non-existence of judicial bodies, prosecutors in particular, in the early months of the war in 1992 and some of the consequences of that. Would you agree with me that one of the consequences of this lack of prosecutors and judges was that -- both civilian and military prosecutors and judges was that hundreds, indeed, thousands of non-Serbs, were being held in detention for months in inhumane conditions and oftentimes guarded by police personnel. That was one of the problems from having no judges and prosecutors; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're looking for a causal link that because there were no prosecutors and judges, what was it again you said? Which number did you mention, of persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Hundreds or even thousands.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collection centres, or whichever way they may be defined, were within the remit of the military bodies. Whatever happened there is because somebody came to those collection centres or because they were kept in a certain area. I wouldn't link the problem of prosecutors' offices to this matter, or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, isn't one of the reasons that those people stayed in detention was because there was no judge or no prosecutor to prosecute the case and the authorities, military, civilian, and police authorities of the RS, were unwilling to release those people. That's what was happening across the Republika Srpska in the early months of the war in 1992. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, talking about the detention, that was the phrase you used, if there were people suspected of committing crimes they couldn't be processed for objective reasons. If that was the reason for their detention, well, we, from the Ministry of the Interior, because there -- unfortunately, there were no prosecutor's offices, released those persons after three days, even though suspected of murder or burglary and robbery and so on which caused great dissatisfaction, especially in those places or neighbourhoods where those people were from, and all that negative energy was directed at the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I've run in a problem sometime in using the term "detention" or "detained," because I understand with the -- with you and other police witnesses, that has a very specific meaning for you. What I'm talking about here are the civilians, non-Serb civilians, who are put in some sort of facility, whether it's a collection centre or a detention facility or a camp, and they're not free to leave and, yet, they're not being charged with any crime, and they're kept for more than three days. And I'm saying part of that problem was because the authorities didn't know what to do with them but they didn't want to release them. That did happen in the early months of 1992 in the RS, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that during the early months. I didn't know the reasons for their detention, nor did I know where they were detained. At least my administration didn't have any pertinent information. We can only speculate about the reasons being for some persons suspected of committing crimes that -- and supposed that they were kept longer than three days which is contrary to the laws and regulations. I didn't have information about the reasons for detention. Only in late 1992, I heard of the existence of some centres such as Prijedor or there were reports from -- from Samac about a facility where a certain number of persons was detained. But those matters basically weren't within the remit of the police so I couldn't say more about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that perhaps you didn't know in July of 1992, but others in the MUP higher ups did know. And to support that, I want to show you Exhibit P160. This is tab 20. And this is about the meeting in Belgrade on the 11th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic did you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were two things. One thing is on page 55, line 11, there should be a witness's answer was recorded as part of your question. So that is one thing. And the second thing is I would like to propose that the previous document, which -- which the -- which the witness commented upon be admitted into evidence because I see there is no -- there is no opposition from the -- from the Office of the Prosecutor, and I showed the document to the -- to the witness and, therefore, I think, because the witness commented on the document, that we should have the document exhibited. It is number 619D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I have no objection. Mr. Zecevic showed it but didn't offer, but now I have directed the witness to a couple specific provisions. I have no objection to it being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 1D661, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you will see on the screen the cover page for this document about the meeting in Belgrade. And I understand you did not attend that meeting. I believe Mr. Planojevic was still the head of the administration, and that was the last one of these meetings he attended.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During -- during your proofing or previous interviews, were you ever shown this document; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't. At least I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to show you one particular paragraph. It's at page 7 of the English in e-court and page 8 of the B/C/S. And the paragraph I want to ask you about Mr. Zupljanin is addressing the group, and I think it's the --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, could I get a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I can hand you the page anyway. Mr. Zupljanin speaking saying: "The army and Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies are requesting that as many Muslims as possible are gathered and they are leaving these undefined camps up to the internal affairs organs. Conditions in these camps are bad. There is no food. Some individuals do not observe international norms because, among other things, such collection centres are not adequate or there are other reasons ..." So it appears that the RS MUP leadership was aware of this situation as of at least July 11th, and the problem with these undefined camps. Mr. Planojevic didn't tell you about this after the July 11th meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I had the opportunity to see this report. Because I cannot see the whole document, probably Mr. Zupljanin relates in it that he had information that the army and the Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies are demanding that as many Muslims as possible be collected and taken to some camps. Whether that was, indeed, done or not, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know that one of the reasons that was being done was that civilian prisoners or detainees or hostages like that could be exchanged for Serbs who were being held by the Muslims or the Croats on the other side of the conflict? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, not in 1992. I didn't know that there were such exchanges. Talking about the Sarajevo area where I stayed, I knew that, through certain structures and if you had money, you could organise for somebody to leave a certain area. But I am not aware of such exchanges as this taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you never hear about the republic commission for the exchange of war prisoners and killed soldiers and others? Were you aware of the existence of that exchange commission in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and the bodies of killed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know a MUP employee named Slobodan Markovic who worked on that commission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you didn't realise that the commission was exchanging not only dead soldiers and prisoners of war but civilians as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the organisation or the powers of the commission apart from the fact that there was a commission called this or that, and I didn't have the opportunity to cooperate with them or to know anything about their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have any more questions about that document for you at the moment. Do you recall a -- a big international furor in the media in the first week of August 1992, when certain information and pictures were circulated about non-Serbs detained in places like Omarska and Manjaca? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I must explain how come. Unfortunately, after leaving Sarajevo and moving to Bijeljina, I got a new apartment, unfurnished, and I had to buy stuff. And only after 1998 [as interpreted] was I in the position to buy a regular TV set and a small radio. And there were no printed media available, especially not international media from which I could get such an information. This is meant more as an illustration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I see you're confirming Mr. Zecevic's remark that it was only after 1993 that you were able to buy a regular TV set and radio; is that right.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to buy a TV set only in 1993, and I did so in a nearby place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you telling me in August 1992 you didn't know anything about those detainees in Manjaca and Omarska and all the international press furor about those camps in Prijedor? You must have heard about it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, in August 1992 up until 3 September, I was in Bijeljina carrying out a specified task, and I was active in respect of the Yellow Wasps so that I didn't have the chance to learn that, especially not from the international media. I couldn't follow those media. Some of us, because simply the shortage of electricity, or for the lack of basic technical means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, were you not aware of Prime Minister Djeric's announcement or reaction on the 7th of August, 1992 responding to a CNN report about Omarska and Manjaca? You didn't hear about that through your police friends or official reports or local media?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. I was dedicated to that aspect and on the storey, or the two storeys where we worked, I don't think there was a single radio set, but certainly not in the office where I spent time with my colleagues. So I couldn't hear anything from the local media, and I'm utterly unfamiliar with the document that Mr. Djeric published or sent to somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when Mr. Tomo Kovac got his position in the ministry as an assistant for police administration for the uniformed police? Do you recall what month that was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall when he first came to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was September, maybe early October. But I think it was September. That's more likely. Mid-September possibly. But I'm not fully certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you attended the MUP collegium or the extended meeting in Trebinje on the 20th of August, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you attended a similar meeting on the 9th of September, on Mount Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the one on October 3rd in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But I'd have to see the document so as not to conjecture. But I think I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there no discussion of this situation about the camps and the civilian detainees at any of those collegiums?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure that it was in September. But I found out that a commission had been established of the Banja Luka centre, and it conducted some checks with regard to the existence of these collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So was that the first time you think you heard about the situation that had existed in Prijedor and Omarska and Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, up until that time - and I think it was September when I first heard of the existence of collection centres - and that a commission had been set up to check some information but not before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think you told us before that you sometimes attended sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go to assembly sessions. In 1992, I may have attended one, but from early 1993 until the end, I attended most every session. But if you're referring to a specific session, do remind me by stating the place where it was held, because only thus can I be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Let me ask you about six or eight sessions in 1992. I think you already said you did not attend the May 12th session in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about the 17th Session which was held 24 through 26 July at the Hotel Bistrica in Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure if I was there in July. But I did attend one towards the end of the year. Perhaps I can help you some more. Being present at an assembly session does not mean being there for three days or sitting in because my role was limited to those items on the agenda that had to do with crime enforcement. Perhaps there was -- there was a question of a member of the assembly and then a reply had to be given or perhaps information had to be presented or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. That makes sense to me. I'm just trying to find out which ones you might have attended to focus on those, if I have a question. But it appears that in most of the assembly sessions, there was at least some discussion of police-related security matters. How about 11 August 1992 in Pale? Did you attend that one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. As you know, I was in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Well, there was one the next day in Banja Luka, so I assume you didn't attend that one either. How about the 14th and 15th of the September in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- are you uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can go on. I'm just making myself more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early September, I think it was around the 3rd, we went to Pale upon the orders of the minister. I don't remember whether we went to Bijeljina and back. But with regard to the Yellow Wasps, there was an order which I remember, pursuant to which we went to Pale in early September. It may have happened that I went there to carry out a specific task, but I don't remember that. And I'm -- really don't believe it was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about the end of October, 30/31 October, 1 November, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend the session in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about the one in Zvornik? 23 and 24 November.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that either you or Mr. Zecevic have asked me about that before, and I answered in the negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one last one in 1992. 17 December, Jahorina mountain.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I was present. Possibly the agenda could jog my memory, if there was an item on it that had to do with the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll have to come back to that later to check for specific items related to the ministry. Now, you talked about a document, Exhibit 1D98. It's tab 20. Defence tab 20. I think it's in your binder, yes. It's a document from the prime minister. I think we have evidence that it was actually signed by the deputy prime minister, Mr. Trbojevic for Mr. Djeric. It's dated 25th of May, 1992, and addressed personally to Mr. Kljajic, asking for a report from the ministry about the situation at TAS, the car factory in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me under what number is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 20, I believe. 2-0. If I wrote the note down correctly. That looks like it. I think that you commented that it was unusual that it was directed to Mr. Kljajic, the under-secretary for public security instead of to Mr. Stanisic, the minister; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you think that one of the reasons that Mr. Djeric, Mr. Trbojevic, did that was because at that time there was some suspicion that Mr. Stanisic may have been involved in that matter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a man and as a policeman with long experience behind me, based on what I know, I cannot believe that Mr. Djeric and least of all Mr. Trbojevic could think that Mr. Stanisic, who has a reputation as a fair and honest police officer, could be involved in something like that. So I can't see how this may have occurred to them. I know that their relations were bad, but the rule was in the pre-war Bosnia and Herzegovina, when the ministry -- when one ministry addresses another ministry or if the government addresses a ministry, then the correspondence is addressed to the minister and not to some of the lower-ranked personnel. That was the general rule. And if there is any suspicion that one of the ministers, the commission was established, the government could establish a commission to investigate any suspicions about the minister. That is why I find it quite strange or perhaps this is just a remark on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I thought you agreed with me that it was strange that it was directed to Mr. Kljajic instead of to the minister and I was asking if that might not be a reason. Do you have some other explanation? Was Mr. Kljajic a personally very close friend of Mr. Djeric? Do you have some other explanation why this was directed in what we agree is an unusual way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why it was sent to Mr. Kljajic, well, I can't say that with 100 per cent certainty. I know that there were some problems between Mr. Djeric and Mr. Stanisic. And it seems to me that in my answer to Mr. Zecevic I gave an explanation to support my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you haven't answered my question: Do you know of any close personal relationship -- oh, would you like to take a break?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a break. I wanted to answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Okay. I guess -- and one of my questions was -- and were Kljajic and Djeric close personal friends, and that's why he might have sent it to Kljajic instead of Mico Stanisic. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that they were close friends. And to my mind, this is a typical example of an attempt to subvert the chain of command by bypassing the minister of the interior and by sending a document, a letter, especially of this kind, to the minister's subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about your testimony at page 22923. You talked about how in May 1992 you and Mr. Planojevic were sent to Kula by the minister. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And apparently somebody in the government or maybe the Red Cross had received information about persons being detained there, some civilians, and you were to go check it out. Why -- why you and Planojevic? You're fairly high up in the system. Do you know why you were chosen for this what seems like routine task?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but I think it was Mr. Planojevic who spoke to the minister, and since at that time in Vrace we had some fuel in a vehicle; I think it was my car. Now, I don't know if it was Mr. Planojevic who made this suggestion or whether it was I. It was maybe 15 or 20 minutes drive, given the conditions. We decided to go there. It was nothing special, really. In my car, I think we had fuel because there were problems with the cars and with fuel and so on, and we simply decided to go. We could have appointed one of our associates, tasked them to go, and the fact that the minister demanded urgent corroboration or confirmation of this information that he received from somebody in the government, that there were civilians in Dobrinja who were moving, withdrawing together with the Territorial Defence from those lines after the fighting ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it turns out these were non-Serb civilians who had been brought in, I think, by TO, Serb TO forces, after some of the combat in the area of Dobrinja; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of mixed ethnic background, or, rather, there were people from various ethnic groups. They were not all non-Serbs. And in this general chaos the information that we received that after the fighting, while the fighting went on, and as the units were retreating, the people were following. They were retreating together with them. That was the information that we got. And they brought them there because they didn't know where else to bring them. They couldn't have brought them back because the fighting was still going on in the broader area of Doboj, Butmir, whatever those neighbourhoods are called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While they were there, who was guarding them; do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say whether they were guarded or not. As we were approaching the duty station, most of them were outside. I don't know if they were smoking or whatever it is they were doing while we were approaching the duty officer to ask him about this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why wasn't this a matter for somebody from the military or the Ministry of Justice, rather than you in the police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was probably a quicker response from a session attended by the minister. He received information, and I don't know if anyone asked him to do anything. I can't speculate. And since at the time we were in Vrace and sessions of the government were held in Pale, he simply called for urgent information by way of confirmation whether this was actually the fact. Now, I really don't know why nobody thought to notify the army to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm ready to move onto another topic. This might be an appropriate pause for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment, to reconvene tomorrow -- Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The witness can be accused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Macar, we have a procedural matter before we rise, so the usher will escort you out ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There's just one very important matter. I refer you to transcript 12791, that was the 13th of July, 2010, and we will all recall on that day, a year ago, that we couldn't believe that Mr. Hannis was turning 39. Today we are equally amazed that he is only turning 40, but we wish him all the best on this special day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the Chamber joins in that sentiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of July, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
